title: Writing Clear Formal and Informal Emails
summary: Learn how to write great emails to friends and to people at work. You will practice using the right words for every situation.

sections.h: When to Use Formal and Informal
sections.p: In English, we change how we write depending on who is reading. Informal emails are for friends and family. You can use short sentences and friendly greetings. Formal emails are for bosses, teachers, or companies. You must be polite and use complete sentences. Choosing the right style shows respect and helps the reader understand you quickly.

ex.en: Dear Mr. Davis, I am writing to ask about the job.
ex.mean: A polite, professional start for a business email.

ex.en: Hi Sarah, hope you are having a great week!
ex.mean: A friendly, warm start for a personal email.

sections.p: The start of your email sets the tone. For a formal email, use 'Dear' followed by the person's title and last name. If you do not know their name, use 'Dear Sir or Madam'. For an informal email, you can just say 'Hi' or 'Hello' with their first name. Always state the reason you are writing right after the greeting.

ex.en: Dear Dr. Smith, thank you for your message.
ex.mean: Formal greeting for someone with a title.

ex.en: Hey Tom, thanks for getting back to me!
ex.mean: Informal greeting for a friend or close colleague.

sections.p: How you end your email is just as important as how you start it. Formal emails need a professional closing like 'Sincerely' or 'Best regards', followed by your full name. Informal emails can end with relaxed phrases like 'Best', 'Cheers', or 'Talk soon', followed by just your first name.

ex.mean: Professional way to end a work email.
Friendly, casual way to end an email to a friend.

tip: Think about your reader before you write. If you would wear a suit to meet them, use a formal email!
